new_statements.translation: ... The semivowels occurring in diphthongs we write e, i etc. In the words of Aghu, Kaeti, Wambon, and in Kati I and II the stress falls on the last syllable; in compound words this can be different, and we then indicate the stress with a grave accent, as we also do in the dialects Sjiagha, Jenimu ... || (p.12) ... compounding of the Germanic 'tree-trunk' type, which one finds in all known Papuan languages, with the stress on the first, the modifying part; since however in this language every word has the stress on the last syllable, in cases such as those in our text this is often not easy to hear; examples of this compounding are: mbüman-mirap 'backbone', ndüàm-wegi 'bamboo knife' ...

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Kaeti (Mandobo) falls on the final syllable of every (non-compound) word; only in compounds may the main stress fall elsewhere (on the first, modifying member of 'tree-trunk'-type compounds), and Drabbe marks such non-final stress with a grave accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in the accessible text.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds: endocentric ('boomstam'-type) compounds carry main stress on the first (modifying) member, though Drabbe says this is often hard to hear because every word is final-stressed; head-first 'type-of-X' compounds (in tomèt, in komütì) and possessor-possessee juxtapositions (u gatèt) stress the second noun; coordinate compounds stress both members (Drabbe 1959:12-13 as reported by Wester 2014:51-53). Any non-final stress is written with a grave accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement ('In de woorden van.. valt de klemtoon op de laatste lettergreep'; 'elk woord'), given in the orthography/sound section of a text-based grammar sketch; Drabbe elsewhere (for Wambon in the same book) calls it a weak accent (van den Heuvel 2025:19). The sentence is a joint statement for Aghu, Kaeti, Wambon and Kati I-II, not a Kaeti-specific instrumental finding.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement is Drabbe's (1959) for 'Kaeti', which Wester 2014:7 identifies as the Rungwanjap dialect of Mandobo (middle Dumut River; main informant a 50-year-old Omba-clan man from the Marek, a Dumut tributary). Glottolog files Drabbe 1959 as the sole descriptive reference under BOTH mand1444 Mandobo Atas and mand1445 Mandobo Bawah, and both languoids carry 'Kaeti' as an alternative name; no page opened here settles whether Rungwanjap falls under Atas (aax) or Bawah (bwp). It is NOT a description of Kokenop Mandobo (koke1241), which Glottolog split off on Jang 2003 intelligibility grounds. Drabbe's sentence is a blanket statement covering Aghu, Kaeti, Wambon (= Yonggom Wambon, yong1280) and Kati I/II (Ok languages) in one clause.

tone_statements.translation: Clean reading: 'Iwam (Upper Sepik) appears to have lexical pitch, Oksapmin has some unexplained pitch features, Duna has two tonemes, the Enga-Huli-Pole-Wiru languages all have lexical pitch (Enga has two tonemes). Awin and Pare seem to have contrastive stress, although Akium-Pare monosyllables possibly show contrastive pitch. Marind has non-phonemic stress, Dumut has non-phonemic stress, but Awyu has phonemic stress (except Aghu, perhaps), Central South Coast has phonemic stress, and Dani has non-phonemic stress.'

sources.citation: de Vries, Lourens. 2020. The Greater Awyu Languages of West Papua. (Pacific Linguistics 657.) Berlin/Boston: De Gruyter Mouton.
sources.note: Ch.2 phonology sketches only Aghu (weak accent on last syllable), Digul Wambon (weak accent on penult), Kombai and Korowai (contrastive pitch accent); no Mandobo word-stress statement. Sec.3.2.4 (pp.28-29): Greater Awyu endocentric compounds have main stress on the modifier; Mandobo and Aghu also have head-first compounds with primary stress on the second noun; exocentric compounds stress both members (cites Wester 2014:51; Drabbe 1959:12, 117).

sources.note: The article is a comparative reconstruction of the consonant systems of Proto Awyu, Proto Dumut and Proto Awyu-Dumut from correspondence sets (Drabbe's 1959 word list plus de Vries' Digul-Wambon and Kombai data, with the author's own Kwem data filling Kaeti gaps). A full-text search of the 22-page PDF finds no occurrence of stress, accent, tone, pitch, prosody or syllable; the only Kaeti phonological statements concern segmental inventory, positional restrictions (e.g. /p/ word-final only in Kaeti), prenasalised voiced stops, word-final m/n alternation (Drabbe 1959:5) and one footnote 'ü: Drab

sources.note: In an areal typological survey of suprasegmentals (which families have lexical pitch/tonemes vs stress), Healey classes Dumut as having non-phonemic stress, i.e. no lexical pitch and no contrastive stress, contrasting it with Awyu (phonemic stress) and with tonal neighbours (Duna, Enga-Huli, Oksapmin pitch features). Second-hand, based on Drabbe's grammars; consistent with Drabbe 1959's fixed final klemtoon for Kaeti.
